Duchenne muscular dystrophy: signs, treatment and daily care

Updated: November 10, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy, usually called DMD, is a genetic condition that gradually weakens muscles. A diagnosis brings decisions about treatment, everyday activities and future plans, but families do not have to solve them all at once. Early specialist care helps protect function, identify complications and support the child’s interests and independence.

What causes Duchenne, and who can be affected?

A change in the DMD gene leaves the body with little or no working dystrophin, a protein that helps protect muscle cells. Muscle is damaged more easily and gradually loses strength. Duchenne belongs to a group of dystrophin-related conditions; Becker muscular dystrophy usually has a milder or later course. These conditions are different from cerebral palsy, which arises from differences or injury in the developing brain.

The DMD gene is on the X chromosome, so Duchenne mainly affects boys. Girls and women with a relevant variant can also have muscle symptoms or heart involvement, and rarely severe disease. A variant may be inherited or arise for the first time in a family. No known family history does not rule it out, and it is not caused by something a parent did during pregnancy.

Early signs deserve an assessment

Signs often become noticeable in the preschool years. A child may walk later than expected, fall frequently, struggle to run or climb stairs, walk on the toes or find it difficult to rise from the floor. Some push their hands against their thighs to help stand, a pattern called Gowers’ sign. Calves may look unusually large despite reduced muscle strength.

One sign alone cannot diagnose Duchenne. Tell the child’s clinician when each difficulty began, whether skills are changing and what happens during ordinary play. Include any speech or learning concerns and relevant family history. Do not assume persistent weakness is laziness or keep waiting for a child to catch up when difficulties are increasing. A pediatric or neuromuscular assessment can establish the next steps.

How the diagnosis is confirmed

The clinician examines strength and movement and may request a creatine kinase blood test, often shortened to CK. A high CK can indicate muscle damage, but it does not identify Duchenne by itself. Genetic testing looks for a disease-causing change in the DMD gene. Sometimes several testing methods are needed; knowing the exact variant also helps assess eligibility for particular treatments.

A muscle biopsy is now reserved mainly for situations where genetic testing has not adequately resolved the diagnosis. It examines a small muscle sample, including its dystrophin. Ask for a copy of the genetic result and an explanation in plain language. Genetic counseling can discuss testing for relatives, possible symptoms in female carriers and future pregnancy options without assuming the same risk applies to every family.

Build a team and a manageable care plan

A neuromuscular specialist usually coordinates care with heart and respiratory clinicians, rehabilitation therapists and other professionals. Nutrition, bone health, growth, puberty, swallowing, learning and emotional wellbeing may all need attention. Ask which appointments are needed now, which can be planned later and whom to contact between visits. Keep a current medicine list and the team’s emergency instructions accessible.

Pain should be taken seriously: Duchenne is not reliably painless. Tight joints, positioning, an injury or another problem may cause discomfort. Describe where it hurts, what makes it worse and whether sleep or activity has changed. New bowel or urinary symptoms also deserve assessment rather than an assurance that they cannot occur. The care plan should address comfort as well as strength and test results.

Corticosteroids need benefits and safety checks

Prednisone or prednisolone and deflazacort are commonly used to slow loss of muscle function; vamorolone is another steroid option in some countries. Treatment may help preserve abilities, but the response varies. There is no promise that a particular medicine gives every child a fixed number of extra walking years. The specialist chooses the product, timing and regimen and reviews them as the child grows.

Monitoring includes appetite and weight, behavior, growth, blood pressure, bones and other possible side effects. Do not stop long-term steroids suddenly: the body may be unable to produce enough of its own stress hormone, causing an adrenal crisis. Ask for a written plan for illness, injury, surgery and vomiting. Persistent vomiting that prevents the child from keeping prescribed steroids down needs emergency assessment. Follow the individual emergency plan without improvising a dose; contact the team urgently for other missed-dose problems.

Other medicines are not interchangeable

Some treatments depend on the exact genetic variant. Eteplirsen, for example, is an infusion used in the United States for variants suitable for exon 51 skipping. Its accelerated approval is based on increased dystrophin, with clinical benefit requiring confirmation. An increase in a laboratory marker is not a guarantee of improved walking. Infusion reactions and other adverse effects also need discussion and monitoring.

Givinostat is a different oral treatment, approved in the United States from age 6. In its main trial, participants receiving it alongside steroids had less decline in measured function; this was not a cure. Monitoring includes blood counts and triglycerides, and clinicians consider diarrhea and heart-rhythm risks. These are examples, not a complete prescribing list. Availability, eligibility and treatment combinations vary by country and individual health.

Gene therapy requires a careful specialist discussion

Gene therapy aims to enable production of a shortened dystrophin protein. It does not remove the need for ongoing heart, breathing and rehabilitation care. As checked in November 2026, the US indication for Elevidys is limited to people aged 4 or older who can walk and have a confirmed DMD mutation. Additional genetic, antibody, liver and other safety criteria apply; meeting the age criterion alone is not enough.

Elevidys carries a boxed warning for serious liver injury and potentially fatal liver failure. Its US indication for people who cannot walk was removed in 2025. Treatment requires extensive preparation and close follow-up, including liver monitoring. Ask about expected benefits, uncertainties, serious risks and alternatives using the current local prescribing information. A news headline or another child’s eligibility cannot establish whether it is suitable for your child.

Heart checks start before symptoms

The heart is a muscle and can be affected even when a child has no obvious cardiac symptoms. Duchenne care guidance recommends cardiology assessment from diagnosis and at least annually, with more frequent visits when indicated. ECG and heart imaging, such as an echocardiogram or cardiac MRI, help guide care. Waiting for breathlessness or using a fixed two-year interval for every child can miss important changes.

The cardiologist may recommend medicines to protect the heart before symptoms appear. Ask what each medicine is for, how it will be monitored and which changes should prompt a call. Female relatives who carry a DMD variant may need their own cardiac assessment even without noticeable muscle weakness; their monitoring schedule is individualized and should not simply be copied from an affected child’s plan.

Breathing and cough strength need regular review

Duchenne can weaken the muscles that move air and clear mucus. Breathing may become too shallow during sleep before problems are obvious in the day. Morning headaches, unusual daytime sleepiness, disturbed sleep, a weaker cough or breathlessness should be reported promptly. Respiratory tests and, when needed, sleep studies help the team decide what support is appropriate.

Some children or adults benefit from assisted coughing or noninvasive ventilation, often initially during sleep. The team teaches how and when to use prescribed equipment and what to do during a respiratory infection. Keep vaccinations and preventive care under review, taking medicines into account. Do not start oxygen or change ventilator settings independently: oxygen alone does not correct inadequate ventilation, and specialist monitoring may be needed.

Support movement without pushing to exhaustion

Physical therapy focuses on preserving comfortable movement, range of motion and participation. The therapist can teach suitable stretches, low-impact activity and rest breaks, and decide whether splints or supported standing are appropriate. Exercises should not be painful or pushed to exhaustion. A generic muscle-building program or insistence that the child walk as much as possible can be unsuitable.

Tight joints and spinal curvature may need positioning, fitted equipment or orthopedic assessment. Mobility aids, including a wheelchair for longer distances or daily use, can conserve energy and increase independence. Their timing varies; there is no fixed birthday when every child stops walking. Review seating, transfers, access and equipment fit as needs change, with the child involved in choices wherever possible.

Nutrition, swallowing and bowel comfort

There is no special diet that reverses Duchenne. A dietitian helps match food, fluids and nutrients to growth, activity and treatment. Some children gain excess weight, particularly with steroids, while others later struggle to eat enough. Calcium, vitamin D and bone health need review, but supplements and restrictive diets should follow an individual assessment rather than an internet regimen.

Report constipation, reflux, prolonged meals, choking, difficulty swallowing or weight loss. Weakness can affect chewing and swallowing, and constipation can add significant discomfort. The team may adjust nutrition, provide swallowing assessment or recommend other support, including tube feeding when oral intake is unsafe or insufficient. Do not force a child to finish food or independently alter food consistency when swallowing safety is uncertain.

Learning, school and emotional wellbeing

Learning ability varies. Some children have language, attention, memory, social or learning difficulties; some have intellectual disability, while others do not. It is inaccurate to promise that Duchenne never affects cognition or to assume that muscle weakness indicates low intelligence. Early assessment can identify a child’s particular strengths and support needs.

Work with school staff on accessible classrooms, rest breaks, suitable activities and learning adjustments. Speech-language, psychological or educational support may help. Include the child’s preferences and friendships in the plan, and ask about anxiety, low mood or coping difficulties. Parents and siblings may also benefit from practical support and time to discuss how the condition affects family life.

Planning for adulthood with realistic hope

Duchenne remains a serious, progressive condition without a cure, but coordinated care has improved survival and quality of life. Many people live into adulthood, study, work, form relationships and make their own decisions about support. A historical age estimate cannot predict one person’s future, and no treatment can promise a particular lifespan.

Ask the team how care will change over time and how to plan the transition to adult services. Useful questions include which treatments fit the genetic result, what monitoring is due, which activities are safe and what practical help is available. Make room for ordinary goals and enjoyable experiences alongside medical planning. Support needs can change without reducing the person’s value or right to participate.

Know when to seek urgent help

Get emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, blue or grey color, collapse or reduced responsiveness. Sudden breathing difficulty or confusion after a fall or possible fracture is also an emergency. Do not attribute a rapid deterioration to the usual progression of Duchenne. Tell emergency staff the diagnosis, current medicines and whether gene therapy has been given, and share the specialist contact details.

Persistent vomiting with inability to keep prescribed steroids down needs emergency assessment, even before the child appears very unwell. Follow the individual emergency plan and do not improvise doses. Contact the care team urgently for other problems taking essential steroids. New severe pain or suspected fracture also needs prompt evaluation. Before any procedure, tell the anesthesia team about Duchenne because some anesthetic medicines can be dangerous. Keep the individual safety plan available at home, school and during travel.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask the neuromuscular team to explain the genetic result, available treatments and a schedule for heart, breathing and rehabilitation reviews.

Keep individualized steroid, illness and procedure instructions with the current medicine list and emergency contacts.

Review comfort, nutrition, school access and emotional wellbeing alongside changes in strength.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help organize appointments, questions and the care team’s written instructions. It cannot diagnose Duchenne, determine gene-therapy eligibility or replace an individual emergency plan.

When to seek help

Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, collapse, reduced responsiveness or sudden breathing or neurological changes after injury. Persistent vomiting with inability to keep prescribed steroids down also needs emergency assessment. Follow the individual emergency plan without improvising doses. Never stop long-term steroids suddenly or change treatment without the specialist team.

Evidence notes updated: November 10, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Duchenne is a progressive genetic muscle condition; girls and women can also be affected.
  • CK testing can suggest muscle damage, while genetic testing helps confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.
  • Medicines have specific eligibility rules, benefits and risks; neither gene therapy nor a diet is a guaranteed cure.
  • Regular heart, breathing, rehabilitation and learning support matter throughout life.
  • Use an individual emergency and steroid plan, and seek help for sudden deterioration.

Frequently asked questions

Does Duchenne affect only boys?

No. It mainly affects boys because the DMD gene is on the X chromosome. Girls and women with a relevant variant can have muscle or heart problems, and occasionally severe disease. Genetic counseling helps families understand testing and monitoring.

What early signs should I mention to the doctor?

Frequent falls, delayed walking, difficulty running or climbing stairs, toe walking or using the hands to push up from the floor are reasons for assessment. Enlarged calves or speech delays may also occur. These signs do not prove Duchenne on their own.

Is there a cure for Duchenne?

There is currently no cure. Medicines and coordinated supportive care can slow aspects of progression, treat complications and improve daily life. New treatments have eligibility restrictions and risks, so decisions need a specialist familiar with the child’s genetic result and health.

How can I support my child day to day?

Follow the agreed treatment and review plan, use therapist-guided activity and equipment, and support nutrition, learning and friendships. Report changes in comfort, breathing, eating or abilities. The aim is participation and wellbeing, not forcing the child to meet someone else’s physical targets.

Does a high CK result mean my child has Duchenne?

No. It signals possible muscle damage and needs interpretation. Genetic testing and specialist assessment help identify the cause; a muscle biopsy is considered only when needed.

Will every child need a wheelchair at age 12?

No fixed age applies. Function and treatment response vary, and mobility equipment may first be useful for longer distances. A wheelchair can support independence and conserve energy rather than represent a failure of care.

Can we stop steroids if side effects are difficult?

Contact the prescribing team to discuss side effects and possible adjustments. Do not stop long-term steroids abruptly, because adrenal crisis can occur. Persistent vomiting with inability to keep prescribed steroids down needs emergency assessment. Follow the individual emergency plan without improvising doses, and seek urgent team advice for other missed-dose problems.

Can my child attend school and learn?

Yes, with support suited to their needs. Learning profiles vary, so physical disability should not determine expectations. Assessment, accessibility measures and educational or psychological help can support progress and participation.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
